title: Empirical Evaluation of a Generate–Validate–Repair Loop for Intent→Network Configuration Using a Deterministic Reachability Validator
abstract: We evaluate whether a generator–validator–repair (GVR) loop around a single LLM (gpt-5-mini) increases the rate of correct, safely executable network configurations synthesized from natural-language intents versus plain LLM generation. Following preregistration cns-m2026-01 we executed a paired design (N=300 intents, 600 episodes) where the baseline used a single model-generated candidate per intent (shared-initial) and the guarded condition applied a deterministic reachability validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) plus at most one automated repair. Baseline succeeded in 299/300 tasks (99.67%); guarded succeeded in 300/300 (100%). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00333; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01]. The preregistered target (10 percentage-point absolute improvement) is not supported: baseline performance was near ceiling, leaving negligible room for improvement by the evaluated single-step GVR intervention. We archive and cite execution manifests, scoring traces, provider-call traces, and the initial-master-prompt immutable reference.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) can translate high-level NetOps intents into low-level device configuration, but deployment requires operational correctness and safety (e.g., no unintended reachability changes). Prior work has proposed verifier-assisted or closed-loop architectures for LLM-driven NetOps, yet rigorous, preregistered, execution‑level experiments quantifying the operational impact of such verification–repair gates remain limited. We ask: Does inserting a deterministic reachability validator and a single automated repair step around an LLM increase the proportion of intents that yield execution-validated, safely executable configurations compared with plain LLM generation? We tested this question in a preregistered paired design (cns-m2026-01) and make three contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N=300) comparing plain-LLM generation to a GVR pipeline using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic reachability validator; (2) complete, auditable artifacts (model calls, provider traces, validator traces, hashes) enabling reproducibility; (3) empirical evidence and operational interpretation showing a ceiling baseline and guidance when GVR loops are likely to be consequential.
sections.related_work: Representative prior studies motivated the design: NetConfEval (Wang et al., 2024) evaluates LLMs for intent→config translation; Raptis et al. (2026) proposes intent-validation pipelines for network automation; architecture proposals such as "Wheel of Intelligence" emphasize proposer/verifier separation. Our experiment complements these works by measuring, under a preregistered paired protocol and deterministic validator semantics, whether a single verification+repair gate produces a measurable increase in execution-validated correctness on a controlled task corpus.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study is preregistered as cns-m2026-01 (preregistration SHA-256 recorded in the execution manifest). Design: paired binary outcome per intent (baseline vs guarded), unit = intent, N=300. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination checks, stopping, retry, and analysis procedures were frozen before execution (see execution manifest). Task generation and contamination: 300 intent→config tasks were produced deterministically by the task generator; all selection steps, RNG seeds, and contamination filters are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; hash: 91564bb69ac692e2fbd6321708863d13938309b5433ef1b211541ba5426df990). Shared-initial baseline semantics: for each intent the experiment used a single shared initial generator call (the "shared-initial" candidate) that served as the baseline candidate for that pair; the guarded condition re-used the same shared-initial candidate and then applied the deterministic validator and, only if validation failed, invoked at most one automated repair call per the preregistration. This shared-generation workflow is demonstrated in the archived provider-call traces (example: execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json; SHA-256 = cfd2d0956873ca732f5278c5d9bd64f0ffb008623d7fb52d2958c7769b69a791) and the per-episode responses (example: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt; SHA-256 = 8f38c8becd7e1e36d8902e9ba2f09218baad021d77365b20eb52914a4bdf4080). Validator and repair budget: validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; repair allowed = at most one automated repair call per task (preregistered). The single observed repair call is archived (execution/provider_calls/task-000117-guarded-repair.json; SHA-256 = 4deb410d5736ab332cd5caaf00b16051e5b0aef2276255c0770098f63cb523ba) and provider_call accounting is in the execution manifest (model_calls_used = 301). Scoring: each episode yielded a binary score: 1 = configuration satisfies intent and shows no unintended reachability change in the emulated environment; 0 = otherwise. Analysis: the preregistered executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed exact McNemar two-sided p and bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). All artifacts and hashes are recorded in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json).
sections.results: Primary confirmatory outcome (artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA-256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55): complete_pair_count = 300. Baseline (shared-initial candidate accepted without repair) successes = 299/300 (99.67%); guarded (validator ± one repair) successes = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 299, n10 = 1 (guarded=1, baseline=0), n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimated paired difference = 0.00333. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Provider-call accounting (execution manifest): model_calls_used = 301; shared_initial_generation = 300; repair calls = 1 (execution/provider_calls/task-000117-guarded-repair.json; SHA-256 given above). Sensitivity / realized detectability: the preregistration targeted a 10 percentage-point absolute improvement (Δ = 0.10). For paired binary outcomes with N=300, an all-one-sided-discordant scenario requires at least k = N·Δ = 30 one-sided discordant pairs (n10−n01 = 30) to produce an observed paired difference of 0.10. The observed discordant-pair sum here is k_obs = n10 + n01 = 1, far below 30; therefore the realized data cannot detect a 10% absolute improvement — numerically, observing a 10% paired increase would require at least 30 discordant pairs, whereas we observed only 1. This arithmetic statement follows directly from the paired-count definitions (contingency table archived at analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Missingness/technical failures: none (failed_episode_count = 0; see execution manifest).
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the baseline LLM (shared-initial candidate) produced near-ceiling correct configurations on this deterministically generated task set; consequently the evaluated single-step GVR loop produced one additional success out of 300. The small absolute improvement (0.33 percentage points) is negligible operationally on this corpus and not statistically detectable against the preregistered 10% target. Operational implication: verification+repair gates can correct isolated generator mistakes (as demonstrated by the single discordant case logged at execution/provider_calls/task-000117-guarded-repair.json), but their measurable benefit requires a nontrivial baseline error rate or a task distribution containing substantially harder or more ambiguous intents. Threats to validity: internal—shared-initial design intentionally isolates validator/repair impact on identical model proposals but does not measure effects of independently re-generating candidates under guarded prompts; construct—the validator operationalizes safety as absence of unintended reachability changes in the emulated network (a practical but partial operationalization); external—tasks were deterministically generated synthetic intents and may not mirror human-authored complexity or production heterogeneity; model scope—single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) limits generalization across model families. All such artifacts and counts are archived (execution manifest and analysis artifacts).
sections.conclusion: In this preregistered paired experiment (N=300), adding a deterministic reachability validator and at most one automated repair around gpt-5-mini produced one extra successful task relative to plain-LLM generation. Because baseline was near ceiling (299/300), the preregistered target improvement (10 percentage points) is not supported; the observed data show the GVR loop provided minimal measurable benefit on this corpus. We release full execution and analysis artifacts to support further work; future studies should (a) evaluate distributions with higher baseline generator error rates (e.g., human-authored, adversarial, or out-of-distribution intents), (b) compare multi-iteration repair policies and stronger validators, and (c) quantify cost–benefit tradeoffs in operational deployments.

limitations: Ceiling effect: baseline success = 299/300 limits detectable improvement; detecting the preregistered 10% absolute increase would require ≥30 one-sided discordant pairs (i.e., n10−n01≥30), but observed discordant-pair sum = 1, so the realized data cannot detect the originally targeted effect size.
Task scope: tasks were deterministically generated synthetic intent→configuration examples; external validity to human-authored, adversarial, or production intents is limited.
Model scope: single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not necessarily generalize to other models or fine-tuned variants.
Validator construct: safety operationalized as absence of unintended reachability changes in the emulated environment (a pragmatic but partial proxy for operational NetOps safety).
Repair budget: only one automated repair attempt per task was allowed (preregistered); multi-iteration repair strategies were not explored in this confirmatory run.
